explain.title: Enzymes are catalysts
explain.body: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed. They can therefore act as catalysts without becoming the products of the reactions.

explain.title: Enzymes have a particular structure
explain.body: Enzymes are predominantly proteins and have a three-dimensional globular structure. This structure allows them to form active sites that can bind specifically to substrates.

explain.title: Enzymes are specific
explain.body: An enzyme is specific to the reaction it catalyses and to the nature of its substrate. For example, amylase specifically catalyses the breakdown of starch into simple sugars.

explain.title: Enzymes can need cofactors
explain.body: Some enzymes need additional non-protein molecules called cofactors to be fully active. Prosthetic groups bind tightly, while coenzymes bind loosely and may be released during the reaction.

explain.title: Enzymes work in different places and uses

explain.title: The active site
explain.body: An enzyme has one or more pockets or clefts on its surface. These are called active sites. The active sites are directly involved in catalysis.

explain.title: Lock-and-key model
explain.body: This model was proposed by a German chemist Emil Fischer in 1894. According to it, the active site of enzyme has a fixed structure. explain.title: Temperature and optimum temperature
explain.body: Each enzyme works at maximum rate at a specific temperature called optimum temperature. For most human enzymes, this is 37°C. A rise in temperature can increase molecular movement and enzyme action, but excessive heat can damage the enzyme.

explain.title: Denaturation
explain.body: When temperature is raised well above the optimum, heat breaks bonds in the enzyme molecule. Its globular structure is lost. This is called denaturation of enzyme and causes a rapid decrease in enzyme action.

explain.title: pH and optimum pH
explain.body: Enzymes are sensitive to the pH of the fluid in which they work. Each enzyme has an optimum pH where its activity is greatest. A pH change can affect amino acids at the active site, slowing enzyme activity or blocking it completely.

explain.title: Substrate concentration
explain.body: Increasing substrate concentration increases the reaction rate while there are free active sites. When all active sites are occupied, the enzyme is saturated and extra substrate cannot increase the rate.

mistakes: Do not say that enzyme activity always increases as temperature rises; above the optimum, activity rapidly decreases.
Do not confuse optimum temperature with denaturation: optimum temperature is where activity is maximum, while denaturation is loss of enzyme structure.
Do not say that all enzymes have the same optimum pH; different enzymes have different optimum pH values.
Do not say that substrate increases the reaction rate without limit; the rate levels off when all active sites are occupied.
When giving the examples, do not reverse them: pepsin works in acidic medium and trypsin in alkaline medium.

explain.title: What is enzyme inhibition?
explain.body: Certain substances, called enzyme inhibitors, bind to enzyme and decrease its activity. This phenomenon is known as enzyme inhibition.

explain.title: Competitive inhibition
explain.body: Some inhibitors resemble the enzyme’s substrate. They compete with the substrate to attach to the active site of enzyme. When the inhibitor is attached to the active site, it blocks it and does not allow the substrate to attach. Antibiotics are examples.

explain.title: Non-competitive inhibition
explain.body: Some inhibitors do not resemble the substrate and do not attach to the active site. They attach at another location, changing the shape of the enzyme and its active site. The substrate then does not fit. Heavy metals like mercury and certain drugs used in cancer therapy are examples.

explain.title: The key difference

example.question: Compare the Lock-and-Key and Induced Fit models of enzyme action.
example.answer: In the Lock-and-Key model, the enzyme’s active site has a fixed shape complementary to the substrate, which fits it like a key in a lock. In the Induced Fit model, the active site is flexible and changes shape as the substrate binds. Both models explain enzyme-substrate specificity and the formation of an enzyme-substrate complex. After the reaction, products leave and the enzyme can be used again. The labelled diagram should show a fixed active site for Lock-and-Key and a changing active site for Induced Fit.

explain.title: Metabolism has two directions
explain.body: Metabolism is the sum of the chemical reactions in a living organism. Catabolism breaks complex molecules down and releases energy. Anabolism builds complex molecules and requires energy.

explain.title: Enzymes are biological catalysts
explain.body: Enzymes are primarily proteins that speed up chemical reactions without being consumed. Their active sites bind particular substrates, which makes enzyme action specific.

explain.title: Enzyme activity depends on conditions
explain.body: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and optimum pH at which it works fastest. Temperature and pH changes can reduce activity; extreme conditions can change the active site and denature the enzyme.

explain.title: Substrate concentration affects reaction rate
explain.body: As substrate concentration rises, activity increases because more substrate molecules can reach active sites. Once the active sites are saturated, the rate reaches a maximum.

explain.title: Inhibitors reduce enzyme action
explain.body: A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site and competes with the substrate. A non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and can change the enzyme’s shape or activity.

explain.title: Two models explain enzyme-substrate binding
explain.body: The Lock-and-Key model describes a fixed active site that matches its substrate. The Induced Fit model describes an active site that changes shape as the substrate binds.

mistakes: Do not say enzymes are used up in the reaction; they can be used again.
Do not say enzyme activity always decreases as temperature rises. It usually rises up to the optimum, then may fall as the enzyme denatures.
Do not confuse optimum pH with a pH that suits every enzyme; different enzymes have different optima.
Do not describe a competitive inhibitor as binding somewhere other than the active site.
Do not say increasing substrate concentration raises the rate forever; the rate levels off when active sites are saturated.
In a comparison, do not reverse the models: Lock-and-Key has a fixed active site, while Induced Fit has a changing active site.

notes.title: Metabolism: breaking down and building up
notes.answer: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions that occur within an organism to sustain life.
notes.explanation: Metabolism includes all the chemical reactions that keep an organism alive. Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy. Anabolism builds complex molecules from simpler ones and uses energy.
notes.simple: Catabolism breaks things down and releases energy. Anabolism builds things up and needs energy.
examples: Cellular respiration breaks glucose into carbon dioxide and water to get energy.
Photosynthesis joins carbon dioxide and water to make glucose using sunlight.
steps: Identify whether complex molecules are being broken down or built up.
If they are broken down into simpler ones, the process is catabolism and releases energy.
If simpler molecules are joined to form complex ones, the process is anabolism and consumes energy.
notes.checkQuestion: Which type of metabolism builds complex molecules and uses energy?
notes.checkAnswer: Anabolism requires energy input; photosynthesis is an example.

notes.title: Enzymes: catalysts with specific jobs
notes.answer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions without being consumed.
notes.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they speed up reactions in living organisms without being used up. Their shape gives them an active site that binds particular substrates, so enzymes are specific. Some enzymes also need cofactors to work fully.
notes.simple: An enzyme is like a reusable helper: it speeds up a particular reaction, then can be used again.
examples: Amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch into simple sugars.
Protease enzymes help remove protein stains from clothes.
steps: A substrate binds to the enzyme’s matching active site.
The enzyme speeds up the reaction.
The product is released, and the enzyme is not consumed.
notes.checkQuestion: Which enzyme breaks down starch into simple sugars?
notes.checkAnswer: Amylase breaks down starch into simple sugars.

notes.title: How Enzymes Act
notes.explanation: An enzyme acts on a substrate at its active site. In the lock-and-key model, the active site has a fixed structure. In the induced fit model, the active site changes shape when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
notes.simple: The active site is the part of an enzyme where the substrate fits and the reaction happens. The two models explain whether that site stays fixed or changes shape.
examples: Lock-and-key: a substrate fits into a fixed active site.
Induced fit: the active site reshapes when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
steps: Identify the enzyme's active site.
Describe how the substrate interacts with that site.
State whether the active site is fixed or reshaped.
Explain that the enzyme catalyzes the reaction and the product is released.
notes.checkQuestion: In which model is the active site reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme?
notes.checkAnswer: The lock-and-key model has a fixed active site; in the induced fit model, the active site is reshaped.

notes.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
notes.answer: The activity of an enzyme is affected by temperature, pH and substrate concentration.
notes.explanation: Enzyme activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration. Each enzyme has conditions where it works best. Too much heat or a big change in pH can reduce its activity, while adding substrate increases the rate only until all enzyme active sites are occupied.
notes.simple: Enzymes work best under particular conditions. If the conditions are not right, they work more slowly or may stop working.
examples: Most human enzymes work fastest at about 37°C.
Pepsin works in an acidic medium, while trypsin works in an alkaline medium.
steps: At a suitable temperature, increasing temperature makes molecules move more and the reaction rate rises.
Above the optimum temperature, heat breaks bonds in the enzyme and its globular structure is lost.
A pH change can affect amino acids at the enzyme's active site and slow or stop the enzyme.
Increasing substrate concentration raises the reaction rate until all active sites are occupied.
Once all active sites are occupied, extra substrate does not increase the reaction rate.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the reaction rate when all enzyme active sites are occupied?
notes.checkAnswer: The rate increases at first, then levels off when all active sites are occupied.

notes.title: How enzyme inhibitors work
notes.answer: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches somewhere other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape.
notes.explanation: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and compete for the enzyme’s active site. Non-competitive inhibitors attach somewhere else on the enzyme; this changes the enzyme’s shape and its active site, so the substrate cannot fit.
notes.simple: An inhibitor slows or blocks an enzyme. It either blocks the active site directly or changes its shape from another place.
examples: An antibiotic can act as a competitive inhibitor of a bacterial enzyme.
Mercury can act as a non-competitive inhibitor.
steps: Check whether the inhibitor resembles the substrate.
If it competes for the active site, it is competitive inhibition.
If it attaches elsewhere and changes the enzyme’s shape, it is non-competitive inhibition.
notes.checkQuestion: Where does a non-competitive inhibitor attach?
notes.checkAnswer: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches somewhere other than the active site and changes the enzyme’s shape.

notes.title: Enzymes: how they work and what affects them
notes.answer: A competitive inhibitor binds to the enzyme’s active site.
notes.explanation: This chapter covers metabolism, enzyme structure and specificity, factors affecting enzyme activity, and inhibition. The exercise text provided here contains Sections A–C; no Section D questions were supplied.
notes.simple: An enzyme is a protein that helps a chemical reaction happen faster. Its active site fits a particular substrate, rather like a shape fitting into a matching space.
examples: Pepsin works best in an acidic environment, while trypsin works best in an alkaline environment.
steps: A substrate binds to the enzyme’s active site.
The enzyme helps convert the substrate into product or products.
The products leave, and the enzyme can be used again.
Temperature, pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors can affect the rate.
notes.checkQuestion: Where does a competitive inhibitor bind to an enzyme?
notes.checkAnswer: A competitive inhibitor binds to the enzyme’s active site and blocks the substrate from binding.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes metabolism?
options: The sum of all chemical reactions within an organism to sustain life
The breakdown of food only in the stomach
The release of energy from sunlight only
The movement of substances into and out of cells
rationales: This is the definition of metabolism.
Metabolism includes many reactions in the organism, not only digestion in the stomach.
Sunlight is involved in photosynthesis, but metabolism includes all chemical reactions that sustain life.
Movement across cell membranes is not the definition of metabolism.

quiz.stem: Which description matches catabolism?
options: Complex molecules are built from simpler ones and energy is consumed.
Complex molecules are broken into simpler ones and energy is released.
Water is removed from an organism without a chemical reaction.
Energy is released without any molecules changing.
rationales: This describes anabolism, which builds complex molecules and consumes energy.
Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler ones and releases energy.
This does not describe the chemical breakdown of complex molecules.
Catabolism involves chemical reactions in which molecules are broken down.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of catabolism?
options: Lipolysis
Protein synthesis
Photosynthesis
Building a complex molecule from smaller units
rationales: Lipolysis breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol, so it is catabolism.
Protein synthesis joins amino acids to form proteins, so it is anabolism.
Photosynthesis joins carbon dioxide and water to make glucose, so it is anabolism.
Building a complex molecule from smaller units describes anabolism.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes cellular respiration as a catabolic process?
options: It breaks glucose into carbon dioxide and water to get energy.
It joins amino acids to form proteins.
It joins carbon dioxide and water to make glucose.
It forms a larger molecule from smaller units using energy.
rationales: Cellular respiration breaks glucose into simpler products to get energy.
Joining amino acids to form proteins is anabolism.
Making glucose from carbon dioxide and water is photosynthesis, an anabolic process.
This is the general description of anabolism, not cellular respiration.

quiz.stem: What happens to energy during anabolism?
options: It consumes energy.
It always releases energy.
It breaks complex molecules into simpler ones.
It changes glucose into carbon dioxide and water.
rationales: Anabolism consumes energy while building complex molecules.
Releasing energy is associated with catabolism.
Breaking complex molecules into simpler ones describes catabolism.
This describes cellular respiration, a catabolic process.

quiz.stem: Which process is correctly matched with catabolism?
options: A lipid is broken into fatty acids and glycerol.
Amino acids are joined to form a protein.
Carbon dioxide and water are joined to make glucose.
Simple units combine to make a larger molecule.
rationales: Lipolysis breaks a lipid into fatty acids and glycerol, making it catabolism.
Joining amino acids builds a protein, so it is anabolism.
Making glucose from smaller substances is anabolism.
Combining smaller units to form a larger molecule describes anabolism.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the role of an enzyme?
options: They speed up reactions without being consumed.
They are consumed as the reaction proceeds.
They store energy for the cell.
They turn into the products of every reaction.
rationales: Correct: enzymes speed up reactions without being consumed in the process.
Incorrect: enzymes are not used up by the reactions they catalyse.
Incorrect: storing energy is not the role of enzymes described in this section.
Incorrect: an enzyme is not changed into the products of every reaction.

quiz.stem: Enzymes are predominantly which type of molecule?
options: A carbohydrate
A protein
A lipid
A metal ion
rationales: Incorrect: the section describes enzymes as predominantly proteins, not carbohydrates.
Correct: enzymes are predominantly proteins.
Incorrect: the section does not describe enzymes as predominantly lipids.
Incorrect: metal ions can be inorganic cofactors, but they are not the main chemical nature of enzymes.

quiz.stem: What is a substrate in an enzyme-controlled reaction?
options: A molecule that binds to an enzyme and undergoes an enzyme-controlled reaction
A molecule that always inhibits an enzyme
A protein that makes up a ribosome
A product released by every enzyme
rationales: Correct: a substrate is a molecule that undergoes an enzyme-controlled reaction.
Incorrect: a substrate is not defined as an inhibitor.
Incorrect: a substrate is not defined as a ribosome protein.
Incorrect: a substrate is acted on in the reaction; it is not the product released.

quiz.stem: What is the importance of an enzyme’s active site?
options: It binds specifically to a substrate.
It is where the enzyme is consumed.
It is a coenzyme released during every reaction.
It is the product of the reaction.
rationales: Correct: the globular structure allows active sites to bind specifically to substrates.
Incorrect: enzymes are not consumed in the reactions they catalyse.
Incorrect: an active site is not a coenzyme.
Incorrect: an active site is part of the enzyme, not the product.

quiz.stem: Where do intracellular enzymes operate?
options: They operate within cells.
They are always secreted into the stomach cavity.
They only function in the paper industry.
They are released during every reaction.
rationales: Correct: intracellular enzymes operate within cells.
Incorrect: enzymes secreted into the stomach cavity are an example of extracellular enzymes.
Incorrect: the paper industry is an application, not the location that defines intracellular enzymes.
Incorrect: enzymes are not defined by being released during every reaction.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes prosthetic groups?
options: They bind tightly to enzymes.
They bind loosely and may be released during the reaction.
They are always metal ions.
They are the substrates of all enzymes.
rationales: Correct: prosthetic groups bind tightly to enzymes.
Incorrect: loose binding and possible release describe coenzymes.
Incorrect: metal ions are examples of inorganic cofactors, not the definition of prosthetic groups.
Incorrect: prosthetic groups are cofactors, not substrates of all enzymes.

quiz.stem: Which is the section’s example of an intracellular enzyme location?
options: Stomach-wall cells secrete enzymes into the stomach cavity.
Enzymes of cellular respiration work within cells.
Amylase breaks down starch into simple sugars.
Protease enzymes remove protein stains from clothes.
rationales: Incorrect: enzymes secreted into the stomach cavity are extracellular.
Correct: enzymes of cellular respiration are given as an example of intracellular enzymes.
Incorrect: this is an example of enzyme specificity, not the stated intracellular example.
Incorrect: this is an industrial use of enzymes, not the stated intracellular example.

quiz.stem: Which industrial use of an enzyme matches the section?
options: Amylase is used to remove resistant starch residues in dish washing.
Protease is used to lower starch viscosity in paper making.
Coenzymes are used to produce white bread.
Ribozymes are used to remove protein stains from clothes.
rationales: Correct: amylase enzymes are used in dish washing to remove resistant starch residues.
Incorrect: the section says enzymes degrade starch to lower viscosity in paper making; it does not identify protease for this use.
Incorrect: the section describes enzymes that break down starch as used in producing white bread, not coenzymes.
Incorrect: protease, not ribozymes, is used to remove protein stains from clothes.

quiz.stem: What is an active site?
options: A pocket or cleft on the enzyme surface
The product released after a reaction
The whole substrate molecule
A separate enzyme inhibitor
rationales: Correct: an active site is a pocket or cleft on the enzyme surface.
Incorrect: a product is formed in the reaction and released from the enzyme.
Incorrect: the substrate interacts with the active site; it is not the active site.
Incorrect: an inhibitor is not the pocket or cleft on the enzyme surface.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the lock-and-key model?
options: The substrate fits precisely into a fixed active site.
The active site is reshaped by the substrate.
The enzyme is released before the substrate binds.
The substrate becomes the enzyme.
rationales: Correct: the model describes a fixed active site into which the substrate fits precisely.
Incorrect: reshaping of the active site describes the induced fit model.
Incorrect: the substrate interacts with the enzyme to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
Incorrect: the substrate is transformed into product or products; it does not become the enzyme.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the induced fit model?
options: The active site has a fixed structure.
The active site is not rigid and is reshaped when the substrate interacts with the enzyme.
The product fits into the active site before the substrate.
The enzyme is consumed during catalysis.
rationales: Incorrect: a fixed active site is the feature of the lock-and-key model.
Correct: in the induced fit model, the active site is not rigid and is reshaped during interaction with the substrate.
Incorrect: the model describes the substrate interacting with the enzyme, not the product binding first.
Incorrect: this section does not describe the enzyme as being consumed.

quiz.stem: Who proposed the lock-and-key model of enzyme action?
options: Emil Fischer
Daniel Koshland
Louis Pasteur
Gregor Mendel
rationales: Correct: Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model in 1894.
Incorrect: Daniel Koshland proposed the induced fit model.
Incorrect: Louis Pasteur is not identified in this section as proposing either model.
Incorrect: Gregor Mendel is not identified in this section as proposing either model.

quiz.stem: In which year was the induced fit model proposed?
rationales: Incorrect: 1894 is the year given for the lock-and-key model.
Correct: Daniel Koshland proposed the induced fit model in 1958.
Incorrect: this year is not given for either model in the section.
Incorrect: this year is not given for either model in the section.

quiz.stem: What forms when the substrate fits into the enzyme's active site in the lock-and-key model?
options: The enzyme-substrate complex
The active site
The product
The substrate alone
rationales: Correct: the substrate and enzyme form an enzyme-substrate complex.
Incorrect: the active site is part of the enzyme and is present before the complex forms.
Incorrect: the product is formed after the enzyme catalyzes the reaction.
Incorrect: the substrate alone is not the complex; it must interact with the enzyme.

quiz.stem: After the enzyme-substrate complex forms, what happens in the lock-and-key model?
options: It catalyzes the reaction, and the substrate is transformed into product or products.
It changes the product back into the substrate.
It permanently holds the product at the active site.
It becomes the substrate after the reaction.
rationales: Correct: the enzyme catalyzes the reaction, transforming the substrate into product or products.
Incorrect: the section describes the substrate being transformed into products, not the reverse.
Incorrect: the products are released from the enzyme.
Incorrect: the enzyme catalyzes the reaction; it does not become the substrate.

quiz.stem: According to the induced fit model, what happens when a substrate interacts with an enzyme?
options: The active site is reshaped to perform its function.
The enzyme's active site stays rigid in every interaction.
The substrate is released before interacting with the enzyme.
The product changes the active site before the substrate binds.
rationales: Correct: the active site is reshaped to perform its function.
Incorrect: the induced fit model states that the active site is not rigid.
Incorrect: the substrate interacts with the enzyme before the reaction produces products.
Incorrect: the section says the substrate interaction reshapes the active site.

quiz.stem: At which temperature do most human enzymes have their optimum activity?
rationales: Correct: the section gives 37°C as the optimum temperature for most human enzymes.
Incorrect: 0°C is not the stated optimum for most human enzymes.
Incorrect: temperatures well above the optimum can denature enzymes.
Incorrect: 50°C is above the stated optimum and can damage many human enzymes.

quiz.stem: What can happen when an enzyme is heated well above its optimum temperature?
options: The enzyme is used up.
The enzyme's globular structure is lost.
The substrate becomes an enzyme.
All active sites become more specific.
rationales: Incorrect: the section describes loss of enzyme structure, not the enzyme being used up.
Correct: heat can break bonds, causing the enzyme's globular structure to be lost; this is denaturation.
Incorrect: heating does not turn a substrate into an enzyme.
Incorrect: the section does not say that heating makes active sites more specific.

quiz.stem: What is meant by an enzyme's optimum pH?
options: The enzyme's optimum pH
The temperature at which an enzyme is denatured
The amount of substrate in the reaction
The pH at which every enzyme works
rationales: Correct: optimum pH is the specific pH at which an enzyme shows maximum activity.
Incorrect: denaturation due to heat is not the definition of optimum pH.
Incorrect: substrate amount is a different factor affecting enzyme activity.
Incorrect: different enzymes have different optimum pH values.

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly compares the optimum pH conditions of pepsin and trypsin?
options: Pepsin works in an alkaline medium and trypsin in an acidic medium.
Both pepsin and trypsin work best in an acidic medium.
Pepsin works in an acidic medium and trypsin in an alkaline medium.
Both enzymes work best at the same pH.
rationales: Incorrect: this reverses the conditions stated for the two enzymes.
Incorrect: trypsin works in an alkaline medium, not an acidic one.
Correct: pepsin works in an acidic medium and trypsin in an alkaline medium.
Incorrect: the section gives different optimum pH values for different enzymes.

quiz.stem: What happens when substrate concentration becomes high enough to occupy all the enzyme active sites?
options: The reaction rate increases without limit.
All active sites become occupied, so extra substrate does not increase the rate.
The enzyme changes into substrate.
The reaction stops as soon as substrate is added.
rationales: Incorrect: the rate levels off rather than increasing without limit.
Correct: once all active sites are occupied, additional substrate cannot find a free active site and the rate does not increase.
Incorrect: substrate does not change the enzyme into substrate.
Incorrect: adding substrate increases the rate at first; it does not immediately stop the reaction.

quiz.stem: According to the section, what causes enzyme denaturation at a temperature well above the optimum?
options: The active site is blocked by heat.
The heat breaks bonds in the enzyme molecule.
Substrate concentration falls to zero.
The pH becomes neutral.
rationales: Incorrect: the section explains denaturation as a loss of enzyme structure, not simply a blocked active site.
Correct: heat breaks bonds in the enzyme molecule, causing its globular structure to be lost.
Incorrect: substrate concentration is not the stated cause of heat denaturation.
Incorrect: a change to neutral pH is not the stated cause of heat denaturation.

quiz.stem: How can a change in pH affect an enzyme?
options: It can change the ionization of amino acids at the active site.
It always increases substrate concentration.
It makes every enzyme work at pH 7.
It causes all enzymes to become saturated.
rationales: Correct: pH can affect the ionization of amino acids at the active site, slowing or blocking enzyme activity.
Incorrect: pH does not necessarily change the amount of substrate.
Incorrect: different enzymes have different optimum pH values.
Incorrect: saturation happens when enzyme active sites are occupied by substrate, not simply because pH changes.

quiz.stem: How does the reaction rate generally change as substrate concentration increases?
options: The reaction rate increases at first and then levels off.
The reaction rate immediately becomes zero.
The enzyme's optimum temperature rises with every substrate molecule.
The enzyme is denatured as soon as substrate concentration increases.
rationales: Correct: the rate increases as substrate concentration rises, then stops increasing when all active sites are occupied.
Incorrect: adding substrate initially increases the reaction rate rather than making it zero.
Incorrect: substrate concentration does not set the enzyme's optimum temperature.
Incorrect: increasing substrate concentration is not stated to denature the enzyme.

quiz.stem: How does a competitive inhibitor reduce enzyme activity?
options: It attaches to the active site and prevents the substrate from attaching.
It attaches to the substrate and carries it away.
It changes the substrate into an inhibitor.
It makes the enzyme produce more active sites.
rationales: Correct: it blocks the active site, so the substrate cannot attach.
Incorrect: competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the enzyme’s active site; they are not described as attaching to the substrate.
Incorrect: the inhibitor does not change the substrate into another substance.
Incorrect: competitive inhibition blocks the active site; it does not create more active sites.

quiz.stem: What happens during non-competitive inhibition?
options: It binds to the active site and blocks the substrate.
It attaches at another location and changes the enzyme’s shape.
It makes the substrate fit the active site more closely.
It breaks down the enzyme into its amino acids.
rationales: Incorrect: attaching to and blocking the active site is the description of competitive inhibition.
Correct: a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the shape of the enzyme and its active site.
Incorrect: the inhibitor changes the enzyme’s shape; it does not make the substrate fit better.
Incorrect: the section describes a shape change, not the enzyme being broken down.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of a competitive inhibitor given in this section?
options: Antibiotics
Biotin
NAD
Magnesium ions
rationales: Correct: the section gives antibiotics as examples of competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: biotin is given as an example of an organic cofactor, not a competitive inhibitor.
Incorrect: NAD is given as an example of a coenzyme, not a competitive inhibitor.
Incorrect: magnesium ions are given as examples of inorganic cofactors, not competitive inhibitors.

quiz.stem: Why can a substrate no longer fit after a non-competitive inhibitor attaches?
options: It blocks the active site.
It changes the shape of the enzyme’s active site.
It becomes a substrate for the enzyme.
It increases the similarity between the enzyme and substrate.
rationales: Incorrect: a non-competitive inhibitor does not attach to the active site to block it directly.
Correct: its attachment changes the enzyme’s shape, including the shape of the active site.
Incorrect: the inhibitor does not become a substrate.
Incorrect: the inhibitor changes the enzyme’s shape so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes a competitive inhibitor?
options: It competes with the substrate for the same active site.
It attaches at a different location and changes enzyme shape.
It attaches to the substrate rather than the enzyme.
It binds only to the products of a reaction.
rationales: Correct: competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate to attach to the same active site.
Incorrect: this describes non-competitive inhibition.
Incorrect: the section says the inhibitor competes with the substrate to attach to the enzyme’s active site.
Incorrect: the section describes inhibitors attaching to enzymes, not only to reaction products.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of a non-competitive inhibitor mentioned in the section?
options: Heavy metals such as mercury
Antibiotics
Substrates of bacterial enzymes
Biotin
rationales: Correct: heavy metals such as mercury are given as examples of non-competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: antibiotics are given as examples of competitive inhibitors.
Incorrect: substrates are the molecules inhibitors compete with; they are not given as inhibitors.
Incorrect: biotin is given as an example of a prosthetic group, not a non-competitive inhibitor.

quiz.stem: Q7.1. Primarily, all enzymes are:
options: Nucleic acids
Proteins
Carbohydrates
Lipids
rationales: Nucleic acids are not the main chemical nature of enzymes.
Correct: enzymes are primarily proteins.
Carbohydrates are not the main chemical nature of enzymes.
Lipids are not the main chemical nature of enzymes.

quiz.stem: Q7.2. Which best defines an enzyme?
options: A chemical that breaks down food.
A hormone that regulates metabolism.
A protein that speeds up reactions.
A molecule that stores energy.
rationales: Some enzymes break down food, but this is not a complete definition.
A hormone is not the definition of an enzyme.
Correct: an enzyme is a protein that speeds up reactions.
Energy storage is not the main role described by this definition.

quiz.stem: Q7.3. What can happen if an enzyme is exposed to temperature that is higher than its optimal temperature?
options: Enzyme activity rate will increase.
Enzyme’s shape will change, potentially reducing its activity.
Enzyme will speed up the reaction and remain stable.
Enzyme will become a substrate itself.
rationales: Above its optimum, activity may fall rather than keep increasing.
Correct: high temperature can change the enzyme’s shape and reduce activity.
The enzyme may not remain stable at a temperature above its optimum.
The enzyme does not become a substrate because of high temperature.

quiz.stem: Q7.4. Enzymes are specific in their action because:
options: Their active sites fit specific substrates.
They are always proteins.
They are consumed in reactions.
They work only at high temperatures.
rationales: Correct: an enzyme’s active site has a shape that fits particular substrate(s).
Being proteins does not by itself explain why enzymes act specifically.
Enzymes are not consumed in the reactions they catalyse.
Enzymes do not work only at high temperatures.

quiz.stem: Q7.5. Prosthetic groups are:
options: Required by all enzymes.
Proteins in nature.
Loosely attached with enzymes.
Tightly bound to enzyme.
rationales: Not all enzymes require a prosthetic group.
A prosthetic group is not defined as a protein.
A loosely attached helper is not a prosthetic group as described here.
Correct: a prosthetic group is tightly bound to an enzyme.

quiz.stem: Q7.6. How does increasing temperature affect enzyme activity?
options: Increases activity to a point
Always decreases activity
Makes enzymes non-functional
No effect on enzyme
rationales: Correct: activity usually increases with temperature up to the optimum.
Activity does not always decrease as temperature rises; it can first increase.
A rise in temperature does not immediately make every enzyme non-functional.
Temperature affects enzyme activity.

quiz.stem: Q7.7. How does competitive inhibitor affect enzyme action?
options: Attaches with the substrate.
Changes enzyme shape.
Attaches and blocks the active site.
Blocks the cofactors.
rationales: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate; it does not attach to the substrate.
Changing enzyme shape is associated with non-competitive inhibition.
Correct: a competitive inhibitor binds at the active site and blocks it.
Blocking cofactors is not the defining action of a competitive inhibitor.

quiz.stem: Q7.8. An enzyme works best at a pH of 7.4. It is placed in an acidic solution with a pH of 4.0. How will this affect the enzyme?
options: The active site will be modified, reducing substrate binding.
The enzyme will catalyse reactions faster due to increased H ions.
The enzyme will gain additional active sites.
The substrate will become inactive in an acidic environment.
rationales: Correct: a pH far from the optimum can alter the active site and reduce substrate binding.
More hydrogen ions do not necessarily make the enzyme work faster; this pH is far from its optimum.
A change in pH does not give the enzyme additional active sites.
The question describes an effect on the enzyme, and the substrate does not necessarily become inactive.

quiz.stem: Q7.9. What is TRUE according to the induced fit model of enzyme action?
options: Enzyme's active site changes shape to bind the substrate.
Substrate changes shape to bind to active site.
No shape changes occur in active site or substrate.
Substrate attaches the enzyme at a site other that active site.
rationales: Correct: in the induced fit model, the active site changes shape as the substrate binds.
The model describes adjustment of the enzyme’s active site, not the substrate changing shape to fit it.
The induced fit model involves a shape change in the active site.
Binding at a site other than the active site is not the induced fit model.

quiz.stem: Q7.10. What is TRUE about the optimum pH values of the following enzymes of digestive system?
options: Pepsin works at low pH while trypsin works at high pH
Both work at high pH
Both work at low pH
Pepsin works at high pH while trypsin works at low pH
rationales: Correct: pepsin works in acidic conditions, while trypsin works in alkaline conditions.
